The Paris Club, private sector data collection entities like Dealogic, and some export credit agencies supply information on bilateral debt restructurings, syndicated loans and international bond issues, and direct and guaranteed export credits. Their strength is that they offer unique insights into certain types of financing—such as officially supported export credits and market-based lending— that are often underrepresented in other data sets. Their limitation is that the information is fragmented, not systematically compiled, and often not publicly available in a timely manner, creating gaps in comprehensive debt monitoring.
Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture
The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Program operates through a three- tier architecture that progressively transforms granular country reporting into internationally comparable statistics and policy-relevant knowledge, while strengthening transparency at every stage of the process (figure 3B.1).

[idr:p128:text:1] (page 128, chapter None)
[International Debt Report 2026 | Chapter 3. Advancing Debt Transparency | printed page 104 (PDF page 128)]
This process also works in reverse. Transparency gaps, new financing instruments, emerging vulnerabilities, and methodological challenges identified through IDS and IDR analysis feed directly back into the DRS. They inform improvements in reporting requirements, classifications, validation rules, reconciliation procedures, methodological guidance, and engagement with both borrowers and creditors. Debt transparency is therefore not a one-time disclosure exercise but a continuous cycle of reporting, validation, reconciliation, dissemination, analysis, and improvement.
This architecture is also central to the World Bank Group’s broader debt transparency agenda. Greater transparency about the amount, composition, terms, and creditors of public debt is essential for sound debt management, credible debt sustainability assessments, effective restructuring, and informed lending and investment decisions. By strengthening reporting standards, improving data quality, reconciling debtor and creditor records, expanding the information available to users, and identifying remaining data gaps, the DRS provides the statistical foundation on which greater debt transparency can be built.

Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. • A weakening dollar amplified the rise in debt. The dramatic depreciation of the US dollar during the year accounted for 28.2 percent of the increase in LMICs’ external public and publicly guaranteed debt. This outcome reflects an important valuation effect: International Debt Statistics are expressed in US dollars for comparability, including liabilities denominated in other currencies. For several of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing.

Of the $301.8 billion increase in LMICs’ PPG debt stock (external debt obligations of a country’s government and any private sector debts backed by a public sector guarantee) recorded in 2025, at least 28.2 percent can be attributed to the depreciation of the US dollar. Borrowing by the PPG sector of the economy gets reported at the instrument level and in the currency in which the liabilities are denominated or repaid. Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. (Refer to box 1.1 for definitions of debt terms used in this report.)

The increase in private creditors’ net debt flows was driven by an increase in new disbursements accompanied by a slowdown in principal repayments over the same period. New disbursements from private creditors lending to the public sector increased 12.1 percent to $367.8 billion, whereas principal repayments decreased by 3.3 percent to $227.3 billion in 2025. The monetary tightening in advanced economies disproportionately affected the riskiest borrowers, and subsequent monetary easing helped improve market conditions and lower borrowing costs from their 2023 peaks. What is unique about this mechanism, compared to direct lending, is that the principal and interest are serviced from future revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets rather than from Ukraine’s own budget. Those revenues are channeled through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, administered by the European Commission. ERA support extended as loans creates a repayment obligation for the government of Ukraine and is therefore recorded as an external debt liability, whereas the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism represents a financial asset of Ukraine available to service the loan. Under the Debtor Reporting System and international statistical standards—the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, sixth and seventh editions (IMF 2009, 2025) and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014)— this loan is classified as a debt instrument based on the existence of a contractual obligation to repay principal and/or interest, rather than on the expected source of repayment. Accordingly, borrowing remains a debt liability even when debt service is expected to be financed from proceeds of immobilized or seized assets. Those proceeds provide the mechanism for repayment but do not change the nature of the liability. Only where repayment is legally limited to those proceeds and the borrower has no obligation to cover any shortfall would the arrangement require different statistical treatment.
